articles.text: Piedmont School Superintendent Randy Booker recently announced that masks would no longer be required inside schools regardless of vaccination status. As previously indicated, Piedmont School District aligned with Alameda County’s policy. On February 28, the state of California dropped the requirement of indoor masks and allowed counties to follow suit. “I believe Piedmont has been ahead of the curve since the start of the pandemic, providing a fine example to the County of what can be accomplished when a community works together to keep its residents safe. That hard work is now showing results,” said Booker. Booker’s initial announcement used the terms “mask-optional” and “mask-optional environment,” and due to some confusion in the community he attempted to clarify the district’s policy on March 8. “The terms [‘mask-optional’ and ‘mask-optional environment’] were used solely to convey that as of next Monday, students and staff would have the option to not wear a mask indoors - if they so choose - and does not represent an overall ‘mask-optional’ policy. PUSD is firmly aligned with the state and Alameda County’s decision that indoor masking is ‘strongly recommended’ for all individuals while on campus,” Booker stated yesterday. Piedmont teachers will not be allowed to require masks in their classrooms. That decision is up to each individual student and staff member. In the period of February 28 to March 4, there were 18 COVID cases reported by students in the district and one case of COVID among staff members. articles.text: After nine years as Principal of Piedmont Middle School, Ryan Fletcher will be stepping down at the end of the school year. He and his family will be relocating to Colorado where he will take on the role of Principal for a middle school in suburban Denver. “I am so grateful for all that I have learned and gained during my time at PMS. As I begin this next chapter and enter a new school community, I can only hope to feel as embraced and supported as I have been throughout my time in Piedmont.” Fletcher said in a letter to the school community on March 2. Fletcher began his journey in education while still an undergrad at the University of Vermont, as a student-teacher in 2000. Upon moving to California in 2003 he taught 4th, 5th and 6th grade in Palo Alto until 2008. After earning a Master’s degree at Santa Clara University, he became Assistant Principal at J.L. Stanford Middle School in Palo Alto from 2009 until 2013. Since then, Fletcher has been the Principal in Piedmont. Accomplishments under his tenure include providing computers for all students, equitable grading practices, late start bell schedule, an updated homework policy, and a comprehensive 6th grade Orientation Program. Fletcher also faithfully guided middle school students and staff through COVID and the transition to distance learning, a hybrid schedule and the return to in-person classes. “Ryan loves working with and knowing the students at ‘his’ school. He is committed to ensuring that all students feel supported,” said veteran 6th grade teacher Ted Scherman. “I have always found Ryan to be a man of strong character and principle. I consider Ryan a colleague and a friend, and I will miss him greatly,” Scherman added. articles.text: Oakland’s rock star biologist, Damon Tighe is the headliner for the “Topics of Merritt” speaker series on March 10 at 3:30 p.m. at The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living. This freeto-the-public Zoom presentation features Oakland’s charming biotechnologist and urban naturalist who has been featured on local news programs. Tighe will present a talk entitled “Fish and Friends of Lake Merritt’s Waters,” and will highlight the incredible fact that salmon are finding their way back into the Lake Merritt watershed after an absence of roughly 20 years. A public question and answer session will follow his presentation. Since last fall, Chinook salmon have been spotted in East Bay rivers and streams that lead to Lake Merritt, but salmon have not been seen in the lake in over two decades. Tighe reports that they have been showing up this year in the hundreds. In addition, Oakland residents have reported sightings in the lake near Glen Echo where the creek runs alongside the Veterans Memorial Building, by the Laney College football field, as well as a tributary that begins in the hills near Mountain View Cemetery and empties into the northwest branch of the lake, near the intersection of Grand Avenue and Harrison Street. Volunteer groups have been helping provide a healthy fish habitat. The Lake Merritt Institute partners with local citizens and Oakland school students to clean up Lake Merritt’s shoreline and creeks on a weekly basis. Conservationists say these salmon sightings in the lake highlight the much-needed care that goes into conserving Lake Merritt’s amazing, but fragile ecosystem. The return of salmon this year has many people excited and offers proof that we should continue efforts to keep Lake Merritt clean, healthy and Oakland biologist Damon Tighe. well-maintained. Damon Tighe attended Saint Mary’s College in Moraga where he worked on local newspapers while earning a Biology/Chemistry degree. He taught high school in Portland, Oregon and moved back to the Bay Area to work on the Human Genome Project at the National Lab’s Joint Genome Institute. He spent time pursuing an MFA in Natural History and Science Filmmaking in Montana, but returned to Oakland to work on befouls and single cell genomics. He now teaches biotechnology to high school teachers through Bio-Rad Laboratories and is well versed in local fungi, plants and critters of Lake Merritt. The “Topics of Merritt” is a free-to-the-public program of The Lake Merritt – Independent Senior Living. The series is designed to offer interesting and compelling speakers from our community and beyond. An archive of these free talks is available on The Lake Merritt – Independent Senior Living’s website. articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont held its third speaker event in its Defending Democracy Speaker Series on March 1, with a discussion on Election Law and the Supreme Court by Berkeley Law School Dean Erwin Chemerinsky. The upcoming events in this series include “Can American Democracy Survive? An International Perspective,” with Dr. Fiona Hill on Mar 30, and Election Subversion and Disinformation with Rick Hasen on April 5. The series is cosponsored by Leagues across the country in Collier County, Florida; Gunnison Valley, Colorado; Oakland, California; The Pikes Peak Region, Colorado; Portland, Oregon; Pueblo, Colorado; Santa Barbara, California; and Solano County, California. Dean Chemerisnky opened his talk by describing an unprecedented event in U.S. history: the first time an incumbent president tried to hold onto power after losing an election. Donald Trump plotted to have his vice president subvert the election and now 70 percent of Republican voters believe that Trump won the election. Since then, 18 states have adopted laws to make voting more difficult for minorities that will have an effect on our elections in 2022 and 2024. Chemerinsky explained partisan gerrymandering, how lines drawn around election districts have long been maximized to favor either Democratic or Republican results. This is not new, but now it’s easier to achieve more favorable results with the aid of computers to analyze populations and draw maps. He stated, “Partisan gerrymandering is illegal when it dilutes the right to vote.” In 2016 and then again in 2018, partisan gerrymandering was found to be unconstitutional, but the Supreme Court reversed this. In June of 2019, the Supreme Court declared challenges to partisan gerrymandering cannot be challenged in federal court because they are political questions. Chemerinsky considers the Voting Rights Act of 1965 to be the most important piece of legislation to counteract our history of Black voter suppression. Chemerinsky made the point that the Supreme Court gutted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act in July 2021 with its decision in Brnovich v. Democratic National Committee. Section 2 prohibits laws that discriminate against minorities. He pointed out the discriminatory effect of moving absentee ballot boxes and other election changes. While partisan gerrymandering cases cannot be heard in federal courts, racial gerrymandering can as it falls under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. Dean Chemerinsky favors increasing the number of Supreme Court justices and having 18-year non-renewable terms for Supreme Court justices. He feels that 40-50 years on the bench is too much power for one person. He thinks Katanji Jackson Brown is terrific and will be confirmed. Also, 2022 will be a momentous year on the Supreme Court with Roe vs. Wade possibly being overruled and with other cases about states funding religious schools and addressing the issues of businesses refusing to serve same sex couples. Chemerinsky closed his presentation with a lively question and answer session with audience members. When asked by Piedmont League President Lorrel Plimier “What can we do?” Mr. Chemerinsky urged people to vote, get others to vote, and work to get congress to adopt new voting rights legislation. This is nonpartisan work to ensure the people get out to vote and that their votes are counted. To learn more about voting rights and the Supreme Court, please watch the recording of this presentation on League of Women Voters’ YouTube channel: lwvpiedmont.org/youtube.
articles.title: Erwin Chemerinsky addresses LWV in its “Defending Democracy” series

articles.text: Join the League of Women Voters of Piedmont (LWV) on Wednesday, March 30, for a discussion with Dr. Fiona Hill, Senior Fellow at The Brookings Institution at Stanford. The Zoom episode will explore the current state of democracy, from both domestic and international points of view. Dr. Hill is the Robert Bosch Senior Fellow at the Center on the United States and Europe in the Foreign Policy program at the Brookings Institution and member of the Council on Foreign Relations. Her most recent book, There is Nothing for You Here, draws on her personal journey out of poverty, as well as her unique perspectives as a historian and policy maker, to show how we can return hope to our forgotten places. From 2017 to 2019, Dr. Hill served as deputy assistant to the president and senior director for European and Russian affairs on Central Asia, regional conflicts, energy, and strategic issues. Co-author of Mr. Putin: Operative in the Kremlin and The Siberian Curse: How Communist Planners Left Russia Out in the Cold, she holds a master’s degree in Soviet studies and a doctorate in history from Harvard University and a master’s in Russian and modern history from St. Andrews University in Scotland. Dean Chemerisnky opened his talk by describing an unprecedented event in U.S. history: the first time an incumbent president tried to hold onto power after losing an election. Donald Trump plotted to have his vice president subvert the election and now 70 percent of Republican voters believe that Trump won the election. Since then, 18 states have adopted laws to make voting more difficult for minorities that will have an effect on our elections in 2022 and 2024. Chemerinsky explained partisan gerrymandering, how lines drawn around election districts have long been maximized to favor either Democratic or Republican results. This is not new, but now it’s easier to achieve more favorable results with the aid of computers to analyze populations and draw maps. He stated, “Partisan gerrymandering is illegal when it dilutes the right to vote.” In 2016 and then again in 2018, partisan gerrymandering was found to be unconstitutional, but the Supreme Court reversed this. Chemerinsky considers the Voting Rights Act of 1965 to be the most important piece of legislation to counteract our history of Black voter suppression. By Tim Johnson Oakland’s rock star biologist, Damon Tighe is the headliner for the “Topics of Merritt” speaker series on March 10 at 3:30 p.m. at The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living. This freeto-the-public Zoom presentation features Oakland’s charming biotechnologist and urban naturalist who has been featured on local news programs. Tighe will present a talk entitled “Fish and Friends of Lake Merritt’s Waters,” and will highlight the incredible fact that salmon are finding their way back into the Lake Merritt watershed after an absence of roughly 20 years. A public question and answer session will follow his presentation. Since last fall, Chinook salmon have been spotted in East Bay rivers and streams that lead to Lake Merritt, but salmon have not been seen in the lake in over two decades. Tighe reports that they have been showing up this year in the hundreds. In addition, Oakland residents have reported sightings in the lake near Glen Echo where the creek runs alongside the Veterans Memorial Building, by the Laney College football field, as well as a tributary that begins in the hills near Mountain View Cemetery and empties into the northwest branch of the lake, near the intersection of Grand Avenue and Harrison Street. Volunteer groups have been helping provide a healthy fish habitat. The Lake Merritt Institute partners with local citizens and Oakland school students to clean up Lake Merritt’s shoreline and creeks on a weekly basis. articles.text: Second generation Piedmonter Brian Goodhue, PHS class of 2006, moved back to town after starting a family. Goodhue may sound like an average Piedmont dad until you look in his garage and see his 450 horsepower Infiniti G35 drift car. “Drifting is a motorsport where the object is to drive your car sideways, essentially fishtailing through a set course of corners. Instead of driving for speed, the goal is to get through the corners as sideways as you can, without spinning out, or hitting anyone,” Goodhue explained. What started as a fascination and high school hobby in the early 2000s became a serious endeavor. He now competes in pro-am drift competitions with the aim of winning a podium spot in a Shootout competition. Finishing in the top three in one of the big events is the only way to attain a Formula Drift professional license; allowing him to drive in the Pro-Spec series. Goodhue discovered drifting in the early days of its inception in American culture. While reading a magazine called Superstreet, this new concept swept him off his feet. “Superstreet had this article on drifting and I was trying to make sense of what they were talking about because they were trying to describe drifting in words. This was before Youtube so you couldn’t just watch a video,” he said. You primarily need a rear wheel drive car to drift. The rear wheels will overpower the front wheels, carrying the rear of the car outwards to complete the turn Brian Goodhue (left) and his Crew Chief Joe Pramic. The pit crew consists of 2-6 members who have five minutes between runs in Shootouts to make repairs. in a controlled slide. In most cars if you try to burnout or start to slide, only one tire spins. Hence drift cars have a “positraction” or a welded together differential (the last part of the transmission attaching the drive shaft and the axle), to force the drive wheels to spin at the same rate. Due to the style-based aspect of the sport, three judges score runs on a 100-point system. One judge looks at speed in relation to the capability of the car and motor. Another looks at the line taken through the course of 3-5 turns in which the car is never allowed to straighten out. Finally, a style judge factors in intangibles like initiation, fluidity, and commitment. The sport of organized drifting originally started in Japan with Japanese rear wheel cars, like Nissan Silvias (240SX in US). Drifting slowly migrated to the states by members of the U.S. Navy who had been stationed in Okinawa, Japan. The sport’s popIn Shootout competitions the lead car picks a driveable line and the follow car tries to duplicate the run as closely as possible Brian Goodhue drove a 1997 Mazda Miata Turbo from 2015-2019. Since 2020 Brian Goodhue has been driving a 2003 Infiniti G35 sedan competition car. During left hand drift turns the front wheels are actually turned to the right. ularity moved to Hawaii and then to the mainland U.S. “It was very grassroots, it wasn’t well known at all as a motorsport until 2002,” explained Goodhue. One of the first sanctioned events was in the parking lot at Golden Gate Fields in 2003,” he said. Goodhue recalls heading to the parking lots at the former Alameda Naval Air Base to practice and was surprised to find spectators. “The police would watch or try to do it with you, and a lot of them could. Nobody cared back then,” he said. Highway Patrol officers now attend sanctioned drift events with police cars set up to drift, in an attempt to recruit drifters to join the CHP. On the professional level companies including Toyota sponsor drifters, but for now Goodhue operates as a privateer. He estimates that there are fewer than 20 drifters in the state who support themselves solely with their driving. The payoffs for winning events are not large, but the top pros get paid through sponsors for TV time now that events are becoming nationally televised. Brian Goodhue’s Infiniti G35 has a Japanese Toyota 2.5l Turbo Inline 6 engine. “I think there is a lot of room for branding from things not normally affiliated with drifting. What drifting has done just for production cars is amazing. When you see a new car commercial it is drifting. Even a minivan is sliding into a parking spot,” he said. Goodhue’s previous cars were always stylish, including a Mazda Miata convertible sporting a green Hawaiian shirt pattern. His current car, an Infiniti G35, is a rarity in the drift world, being a sedan instead of a coupe. At 6’1” Goodhue likes it for the cabin room, but said, “It is a unique drift car, so there are not many styling options for it.” Goodhue is teaming up with graphic designer Triple Style to design specific paint schemes and designs. “My goal for 2022 is to bring to market a body effect kit for my car and market it through the year as a product specific to my camp, Team Goodhue,” he said. Sonoma Raceway is set to renew its Wednesday Night Drag and Drift weekly events which run through December, and which Goodhue says has helped grow the motorsport tremendously. To try to attain his pro license he will be at Shootout events around the west coast, which were most recently held at Sonoma’s Annual Winter Jam Drift Festival, Thunderhill Raceway an hour outside of Chico and Las Vegas Motor Speedway. Appointees to the Planning Commission are required to submit a statement of economic interests. It provides a financial review of new programs in excess of $250,000 per year. Commissioners still serving active terms include Andrew Flynn, Cathie Geddeis, Deborah Leland, Robert McBain, Paul Raskin, Frank Ryan, Vanessa Washington and Chris Kwei (Alternate). Alameda County Mosquito Abatement District 1 vacancy; 2-year term This position serves as the City’s trustee on the Board of the Alameda County Mosquito Abatement District. Civil Service Commission 2 vacancies, 2 incumbent; 3-year term The commission deals with personnel issues including classification and serves as the hearing board in disputes between the City and employees. This commission meets as required. Incumbent Commissioners serving active terms are Scott Lawson, Amy Kelly, Laura Isaacs, David Hobstetter, and Claudia Harrison. ment-2022 Applications may be sent by e-mail to the City Clerk’s office at JTulloch@piedmont.ca.gov, or delivered in person to Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue. articles.text: Piedmont High principal Adam Littlefield held an online meeting team on Wednesday, March 2 to address the status of the varsity football team. it was the first public declaration to parents that the school is committed to continuing its 101-year tradition of football as a fall sport. “I’ll point it out right now that it is my interest in having a varsity and junior varsity team next year… I didn’t play football in high school, but Friday Night Lights just thrills me, it’s a great opportunity and I appreciate that,” said Littlefield during the meeting. The meeting cleared up some confusion and included a timeline of events on decision making, while offering apologies to parents for allowing rumors to swirl about the possibility of the school not fielding a team in August. Littlefield explained that the school’s Athletic Director Bradley Smet judged that after 11 seniors from team graduated, coupled with injuries, varsity football would not be feasible in 2022. “Player-safety is always our highest priority… This last year we had less than 20 players, where some were playing hurt and some weren’t playing at all,” said Littlefield. On November 12, Littlefield indicated that the school informed other teams in the league that PHS may not field a varsity football team. That resulted in the league forming schedules without Piedmont. A Shoreline Division schedule on December 9 without Piedmont’s inclusion was approved by PHS. “Back in November, Bradley initiated a conversation with the other athletic departments that it was likely that we wouldn’t have a varsity team because we didn’t have enough players. They went ahead with making schedules at that particular time with the caveat that we would be able to field a JV and if we were able to field a varsity team, that was something we could work through as well,” said Littlefield. The principal issued an apology for not sharing that information during the winter months. Moving forward, Littlefield explained that resolving the varsity football situation is now a priority for him ahead of his retirement at the end of the school year. PHS will need the approval of a majority of league teams to be added to the traditional WACC Shoreline schedule. “I can’t undo what has already happened, but I can do my best to move us forward… Two of the teams in the Shoreline Division said they would work with us, while Bradley also reached out to the four teams in the Shoreline which are also aligned in the Mission Valley league, and only one school said that it could not change its schedule,” said Littlefield. Littlefield said that he reached out to WACC Commissioner Dave Kiesel to make sure Piedmont can stay in the league. “I reached out to our WACC Commissioner and I told him there were a few teams who were willing to work with us. He responded that he didn’t want to ‘shut off anything, but it would be difficult based on schedules teams already had,” said Littlefield. Kiesel suggested that Piedmont could fill its schedule with non-league teams, and seemed committed to helping PHS. “There’s also an option that we could schedule non-WACC teams as part of our season. It wouldn’t necessarily be against league members, but Kiesel said he would ‘bend over backwards’ to make that work,” said Littlefield. The next step now is for Piedmont High to hire a head football coach to replace Jerome Johnson. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team opened the 2022 season with a 6-3 win over North Coast section rival Campolindo and a 7-0 loss to Los Altos, a Central Coast Section team. The Highlanders were scheduled to compete in the top division of the California Tennis Classic in Fresno on March 4-5, but the event was canceled due to rain in the city’s forecast. “The tournament was canceled after they expected rain, so we played Los Altos on Saturday instead. Despite the lopsided score, it was a good match and our boys put up a fight. There was a lot of good tennis against a very strong team and this match will help sharpen us up for the remainder of the season,” said coach Jim Landes. In the match with Campo, Piedmont won four of the nine matches in three seats each, clearly a match that could have been won by either team. Sophomore Ben Breber made his first appearance after returning from the basketball team, winning in straight sets, 6-2, 7-6 (6-4) at No. 2. “We defeated Campolindo in a tightly contested match,” said Landes. “Five matches went to the 3rd set and we won four of them. Ben has not let his long basketball season affect his tennis in the slightest. He played remarkably well, blasting forehands and coming forward to finish points and winning in straight sets.” Campolindo win In singles foreign exchange student Lenni Burchardt lost in three sets at No. 1, 6-4, 1-6, 10-3. At No. 2, Breber won 6-2, 7-6 (6-4). Monte Imburg appeared at No. 3, losing 6-2, 6-4. Ethan Pham played at No. 4 and won 6-0, 3-6, 6-4. Olcott breezed to a 6-1, 7-5 victory, and at No. 5 singles, Kai Baudendistel lost in three sets, 3-6, 6-3, 6-4. Piedmont swept all three doubles matches. Playing No. 1, Oliver Maxwell and Nick King won 4-6, 6-1, 6-4; Arun Brahma and Charlie Sullivan at No., 2 won 6-1, 4-6, 6-3; and Carson Hicks and Graham McWeeny won 6-3, 6-4 at No. 3. Littlefield explained that the school’s Athletic Director Bradley Smet judged that after 11 seniors from team graduated, coupled with injuries, varsity football would not be feasible in 2022. “Player-safety is always our highest priority… This last year we had less than 20 players, where some were playing hurt and some weren’t playing at all,” said Littlefield. On November 12, Littlefield indicated that the school informed other teams in the league that PHS may not field a varsity football team. That resulted in the league forming schedules without Piedmont. A Shoreline Division schedule on December 9 without Piedmont’s inclusion was approved by PHS. “Back in November, Bradley initiated a conversation with the other athletic departments that it was likely that we wouldn’t have a varsity team because we didn’t have enough players. They went ahead with making schedules at that particular time with the caveat that we would be able to field a JV and if we were able to field a varsity team, that was something we could work through as well,” said Littlefield. The principal issued an apology for not sharing that information during the winter months. Moving forward, Littlefield explained that resolving the varsity football situation is now a priority for him ahead of his retirement at the end of the school year. PHS will need the approval of a majority of league teams to be added to the traditional WACC Shoreline schedule. “I can’t undo what has already happened, but I can do my best to move us forward… Two of the teams in the Shoreline Division said they would work with us, while Bradley also reached out to the four teams in the Shoreline which are also aligned in the Mission Valley league, and only one school said that it could not change its schedule,” said Littlefield. Littlefield said that he reached out to WACC Commissioner Dave Kiesel to make sure Piedmont can stay in the league. “I reached out to our WACC Commissioner and I told him there were a few teams who were willing to work with us. He responded that he didn’t want to ‘shut off anything, but it would be difficult based on schedules teams already had,” said Littlefield. Kiesel suggested that Piedmont could fill its schedule with non-league teams, and seemed committed to helping PHS. “There’s also an option that we could schedule non-WACC teams as part of our season. It wouldn’t necessarily be against league members, but Kiesel said he would ‘bend over backwards’ to make that work,” said Littlefield. The next step now is for Piedmont High to hire a head football coach to replace Jerome Johnson. Piedmont beats Campolindo 6-3, loses 7-0 to Los Altos By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team opened the 2022 season with a 6-3 win over North Coast section rival Campolindo and a 7-0 loss to Los Altos, a Central Coast Section team. The Highlanders were scheduled to compete in the top division of the California Tennis Classic in Fresno on March 4-5, but the event was canceled due to rain in the city’s forecast. “The tournament was canceled after they expected rain, so we played Los Altos on Saturday instead. Despite the lopsided score, it was a good match and our boys put up a fight. There was a lot of good tennis against a very strong team and this match will help sharpen us up for the remainder of the season,” said coach Jim Landes. In the match with Campo, Piedmont won four of the nine matches in three seats each, clearly a match that could have been won by either team. Sophomore Ben Breber made his first appearance after returning from the basketball team, winning in straight sets, 6-2, 7-6 (6-4) at No. 2. “We defeated Campolindo in a tightly contested match,” said Landes. “Five matches went to the 3rd set and we won four of them. Ben has not let his long basketball season affect his tennis in the slightest. He played remarkably well, blasting forehands and coming forward to finish points and winning in straight sets.” Campolindo win In singles foreign exchange student Lenni Burchardt lost in three sets at No. 1, 6-4, 1-6, 10-3. articles.text: Lacrosse team beats Dougherty Valley 18-8, Berkeley 18-10, College Park 18-5 The Piedmont boys’ lacrosse team is on fire, recording an 18-8 win over Dougherty Valley on Monday, March 7, defeated league opponent Berkeley 18-10 on Friday, March 4, and winning the season-opener 18-5 with College Park on Tuesday, March 1. All games were at Witter Field. “We’re very talented offensively, it’s pretty potent,” said first-year head coach Alex Yu, “We’re riding with it as the team improves. We’ve started the games a little bit slow and usually by the second half, we’re really on fire. That’s when the team shows its true colors.” Monday’s game with Dougherty Valley was a highlight reel performance by junior attacker Nate Fredericks, who scored a jaw-dropping nine goals. He mentioned that some fuel was added to his fire when Piedmont narrowly held a 5-4 advantage at the end of the first quarter after leading 5-1 to start the game. “Our locker room talk (at halftime) was to come out of the gate heavy, so that’s what I did to the best of my ability. I wanted to come back firing,” said Fredericks. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team returns to Witter Field after losing its top pair of attackers to graduation, all-time assist leader Sadie Tschider and leading goal scorer Caroline Devine. In their wake, coach Carlton Chan still expects a team that will compete despite some big holes to fill. “On average, we’re a better team than a lot of years, but we’re without those obvious superstars from previous years. The girls haven’t played together for a long time,” said Chan. Piedmont is still the reigning Division 2 North Coast Section champion from 2019. There are a few holdovers from that team The girls’ lacrosse team. who will be starters: Elizabeth Ethington, Charlotte Theut, and Eliza Keville. The leading scorer returning from last season is senior Katherine Kinne, who had 28 goals and seven assists. Chan said that they will need Kinne to fill the scorer’s role, while they also need people to step up around her. “Katherine is mainly an attacker, but we play her in the midfield. Charlotte is a midfielder, but we’ll play her at defense as Photos by Todd Marshburn well. Elizabeth Ethington is an attacker, Eliza Keville will also play defense – those are our four captains,” explained Chan. Chan had high praise for goalies Sophia Ethington, a senior, and junior Lindsey Kottle. “Our goalie is great, Sophia is keeping up in games and helping us establish ourselves. Lindsey Kottle is a returner from last year as well and they split duty, she’s also a really good goalie. We’re really comfortable with them splitting duties. Goalie-play may be where our strength is,” said Chan. “We have a lot of girls who are very unselfish with the ball and we need them to be a bit more selfish. We need someone to take control and become the star of the offense. A lot of this year’s players were secondary players in previous years. Now it’s their time to take over,” said Chan. The run for Western Alameda County Conference title is likely to be between Bishop O’Dowd, Piedmont and Berkeley. Chan is undefeated against O’Dowd at 6-0. The Dragons hired former Highlanders’ assistant coach Lizzy Koehler to the lead job this year. “This will be one of our closest battles, O’Dowd has a good team and they’ve hired our former assistant coach as their head coach. She’s a good friend; it will be a good rivalry,” said Chan. Katherine Kinne scored 28 goals last season. Charlotte Theut is another senior captain. She scored two gamewinning goals last season, including one against O’Dowd.

articles.text: Senior pole vaulter Parker Terrill is starting the spring track and field season with a clear mission in mind – to be the best. The 17-year-old just set a school record in pole vault with a leap of 14-feet, 2-inches at the Clayton Valley Ugly Eagles Relays in Concord on Saturday, March 5. It broke Marshall Wentworth’s 2011 record by two inches. Piedmont’s top five all-time male pole vault records • Parker Terrill 14 feet, 2 inches (2022) • Marshall Wentworth 14 feet (2011) • Irving Moore 13 feet (1940) • Alex Harrison 12 feet, 7 inches (2016) • John Hind 12 feet, 6 inches (1957) Terrill’s 14-feet, 2 inches would have placed him 2nd in the last NCS Bayshore Championship in 2019. The senior now has his sights set on clearing the bar at five meters, 16 feet, 4 inches. “I knew it was a number that was bound to happen. To get the record felt like a good goal to achieve and now I can continue and break it again,” said Terrill. Terrill started the season at the Skyline Invitational on February 26 with a vault of 13 feet, 1 inch. PHS coach Jeanine Holmlund expects big things to happen this year. “It was so exciting to watch, but he is really just getting started. There’s going to be another one (record),” said Holmlund excitedly. Prior to Terrill’s initial vault on February 26, his only official result was at 8-feet, 6-inches at the Del Campo Multi-Event Competition on May 29 last year. Since then, Terrill diligently worked on his craft and bumped up his numbers in training. “It’s been a four-day week of reps since May, all through the summer, and until now. The process has been a lot of work and dedication,” said Terrill. Terrill is focused on being an all-around track and field athlete and developing himself in the decathlon, which is 10 events that typically includes the 100-meter dash, Long jump, Shot put, High jump, 400 meters, 110 meter hurdles, Discus throw, Javelin throw, 1500 metera, and Terrill’s specialty, the pole vault. “My main goal is to just get better at pole vault. It’s my main event, but I really want improve at the decathlon; there are three throws, two sprints, there’s long jump, hurdles, and the high jump... I really want to prioritize developing as an all-around athlete,” said Terrill. In Clayton, Terrill also helped the 4x400 relay team place 2nd of six with a time of 3:38.66. All four of Piedmont varsity teams reached the NCS postseason playoffs, and the boys soccer team won the school’s first North Coast Section Championship. In addition, three Piedmont athletes were named as League Most Valuable Players: JoJo Murphy, basketball, Trinity Zamora, basketball, and Andre Stankiewicz, soccer. This year’s All-League recipients: Boys’ Soccer The boys’ soccer team finished 15-2-4 overall, won the WACC Shoreline title by going undefeated 10-0-0, and won the Division 4 North Coast Section title as the No. 1 seed in a 1-0 win over University, They advanced in the State playoffs for the first time and as the No. 6 seed lost 2-0 to No. 3 Sacred Heart Prep. They received five All-League selections: Audrey Lam and Morgan Hunt earning first-team honors, Nina Goldberg earned second-team honors, and Tucker Donahue and Cameron Lorin earned honorable mentions. articles.text: The Piedmont Mountain Bike Team began its season on Sunday, February 27 with a trip to Exchequer Mountain Bike park in La Grange, CA. Piedmont had 13 high school and four middle school racers competing, and ended up with Schuyler Sawicki placing 4th place and earning a spot on the podium and Matteo Scanu notching a 6th place finish. Junior Andres Roberts earned a 9th place finish in the JV boys’ D1 category. Next up is a race at Fort Ord, near Monterey. This is a familiar course for returning riders. New riders got to experience it earlier this year with a pre-season race on February 6th.

articles.text: Featured artists at a show at Berkeley Art Museum are Tammy Rae Carland, David Huffman, Lava Thomas, and John Zurier. The UC Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) will highlight the talents of four contemporary Bay Area artists in a collective exhibition beginning March 19. The exhibition is entitled “The Artist’s Eye,” and features guest curation by Tammy Rae Carland, David Huffman, Lava Thomas, and John Zurier. The four artists were chosen by BAMPFA to “guest-curate” an exhibition that draws from the museum’s collection of 18,000 works. Each artist has been featured at BAMPFA in the past. “We’re delighted to work with Tammy Rae Carland, David Huffman, Lava Thomas, and John Zurier, who brought their instinctive curiosity to exploring, curating, and critiquing the collection,” said Curatorial Assistant Claire Frost, who worked with the artists to organize the exhibition, along with Associate Curator Stephanie Cannizzo and Collections Engagement Associate and Academic Liaison Lynne Kimura. “The project required close collaboration on many levels and has resulted in an exhibition that illuminates their work and lived experiences as it intersects with the museum.” The name of the exhibition is a nod to an iconic program at London’s National Gallery during the 1980s, which invited one artist at a time to curate an exhibition from that museum’s collection. A few artists featured in this exhibition include Zarouhie Abdalian, Diane Arbus, Francis Bacon, Yamamoto Baitsu, John Baldessari, Sadie Barnette, Jean-Michel Basquiat, Romare Bearden, McArthur Binion, Yosa Busan, John Cage, Tammy Rae Carland, Theresa Hak Kyung Cha, Constance Chang, Sarah Charlesworth, Barbara Chase-Riboud, Robert Colescott, Willem de Kooning, Erica Deeman, and Jay DeFeo. To learn more and to obtain tickets, visit www.bampfa.org.

articles.text: The Alvin Ailey Dance Company will perform at Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall beginning March 29. Cal Performances at the University of California, Berkeley is presenting the Alvin Ailey American Dance Theatre in six performances at Zellerbach Hall beginning March 29, It is the first time they have performed locally in two years. The dance company, now in its seventh decade, has regularly performed at Zellerbach Hall, and has appeared on the UC Berkeley’s campus more than any other place in the world outside of their home base in New York City. This season celebrates Artistic Director Robert Battle and his decade of tenure with the company. Highlights of the performances at Zellerbach Hall include a Robert Battle 10th Anniversary program; the Bay Area premiere of Battle’s For Four; and the West Coast staged premiere of Holding Space by Ailey Resident Choreographer Jamar Roberts, a Cal Performances’ co-commissioned work given its streaming world premiere as part of last year’s Cal Performances at Home online series. Other highlights of the engagement include the return of hip-hop innovator Rennie Harris’ Lazarus; and an All Ailey program celebrating 50 years of Cry, Ailey’s legendary solo dance; and featuring a new 2021 production of the Duke Ellington-inspired Pas de Duke. Tickets are available through the Ticket Office at Zellerbach Hall, at (510) 642-9988, by e-mail at calperformances.org, and at the door. For more information visit calperformances.org/discounts.

articles.text: After the swing and bebop eras in the thirties and forties, jazz mellowed and became harmonically simpler with cool jazz, west coast jazz, then modal jazz. With arrangers like Gil Evans (Miles Davis’ arranger) and George Russell (author of The Lydian Chromatic Concept), arrangements became clearer and more uniform, making the melody easier to hear. Chord durations were much longer, giving the improviser more freedom to periodically deviate from the current chord. A decade later, jazz fusion guitarists John Scofield, Pat Martino, Scott Henderson, Allan Holdsworth and other jazz fusion guitarists expanded what is aurally acceptable to listeners with innovative harmonic, melodic and rhythmic design. They have all used chromatic drift, where bits of pentatonic scales, diatonic scales, arpeggios and melodic themes can reoccur a half step up or down and return. Chromatic drift establishes brief secondary keys. Voice leading is used to return to the original key with chromatic tones and common tones. Not everyone likes chromatic drift. They tend to love it or hate it. Look at it as an intense spice and use it sparingly and set it up to make sense. Upon first hearing chromatic drift, it may sound out of key or atonal. Once the listener realizes that the accompaniment has not deviated from the current chord, brief instances of chromatic drift can become acceptable and the harmonic deviation seems intentional. John Scofield has played in a diversity of styles, including traditional jazz, funk, rock and blues. He’s performed with Miles Davis, Herbie Hancock, Pat Metheny, Phil Lesh (Grateful Dead) and John Mayer. From all these associations, he picked up ways to play “outside” the key and return while still making sense. Pat Martino and Pat Metheny are among the first guitarists (1970’s) to arpeggiate an interval of a third and move it up or down chromatically. That’s now commonplace for modern jazz guitarists. You can read about various short melodic themes called melodic cells at this web address: http://guitarimprov.com/zc-Melodic_Cells.pdf On the score for the chromatic drift example (link below), there are annotations below the standard notation staff to show superimposed chords and scales that are played. While the main chord is “C7”, the melody may play brief melodic cells to represent Cm7 (darkened C7), Bm7, Bbm7 then Cm7 again. Before becoming to questionable harmonically, the tonality returns to the original key. Use a “two second rule”: if your deviation from the current chord is shorter than two seconds, the listener won’t hear the harmonic disagreement long enough to identify it as too dissonant. The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet A discussion was begun, and the students tried to name the children of Johann Sebastian Bach. The students named the most notable musical children of Bach. I contributed the name PDQ Bach. Michael, who is sitting next to me, looked at me and said Michael Tilson Thomas - “Did you ever hear of Professor Peter Schickele?” It didn’t take before he was MTT a mastermind for me to realize I had made a tremendous blunder. I pretended that I knew who he was talking about but, in reality, I had absolutely no idea who Peter Schickele was. Michael was a brilliant student. He devised a system to remember all kinds of things. We were studying medieval music. In order to remember the musical form of a Virelai, Michael used the sentence “Achilles became bald at Athens.” That was his easy way to remember the form, which is AbbaA. One time a group of music students were just sitting around chatting. In the group were noted violinists Michael Foxman, Pierre Amoyal, and a very attractive cellist. The young lady mentioned that she found MTT attractive but mentioned that he never asked her out on a date. Pierre looked at me and said “Joe, explain it to her.” Her eyes opened wide and I don’t think she understood a thing I said. When people think of Michael Tilson Thomas, they do not think of him as a tough guy. But he was. I was backstage with him during the intermission of a concert. articles.text: A Most Violent Year, released in 2014, is an elegant and beautifully constructed film, one in which the title is unfortunate because the violence, while implied and certainly embedded in the narrative, is never gratuitous. The year is 1981; New York City is in the throes of a hardedged crime wave that is felt in all corners of the city and creates a context and backdrop, contributing to the atmospherics of a taut and cerebral story. At the film’s center are Abel Morales (Oscar Isaac), a seemingly decent and impeccably dressed Colombian immigrant and his elegant but steely wife Anna (Jessica Chastain). Together they own a home heating oil business – a stable of trucks and drivers – based in one of the outer New York boroughs along the East River. They are in the process of acquiring a valuable piece of real estate adjoining their business, have purchased an option from a cohort of Orthodox Jews who have no use for the land or the oil tanks. Abel and Anna have 30 days to close the escrow and need an additional $1.5 million to fulfill the terms of the agreement. If they fail to close, they lose their deposit and the much-coveted property. Writer/director J.C. Chandor nicely inserts a game clock of sorts that gives the film an added tension. From the minute Abel hands the Rabbi a suitcase of cash, events begin conspiring to prevent Abel from meeting the deadline. Most disconcerting (at least at the outset) is that his heating oil trucks, filled with product and on the way to making deliveries, are being hijacked. The question is by whom? His competitors? Abel soon learns from his lawyer, Andrew Walsh (Albert Brooks), that the local D.A., intent on making his bones, is investigating the company and is threatening to indict Abel and Anna for fraud and tax evasion (charges that seem constructed out of whole cloth). Abel’s bank loan of $1.5 million is in jeopardy due to their legal troubles as well as the hijackings. Abel and Anna are caught in a nexus of circumstances that threaten them and their two young girls. It’s a perfect storm of existential events. Compounding their financial situation, they’ve also just bought a new, decidedly modern home in Westchester. The film is ultimately a character study of Abel and Anna, examining intently what they are and are not prepared to do to salvage their situation and what lines they will and will not cross. Abel reminds Anna that he will not become a “gangster” in order to survive in what is a bare knuckles business, one that is, historically, layered with Mob control. A Most Violent Year demonstrates that a film can be a hammer but not every scene need be a nail. It is nuanced and subtle, the tone quietly chilly, the photography often soft instead of hard-edged with wide-angle shots of the Manhattan skyline and snow-covered stretches of land. Violent, when closely watched, is a far more interesting and complex tale when compared to, say, Martin Scorsese’s extreme The Wolf of Wall Street or Goodfellas. One film that it does borrow from in complexity and inherent ambivalence is The Godfather. To quote a line by Michael Corleone “Just when I think I’m out, they pull me back in.” And so it is with Abel Morales. A Most Violent Year. Directed by J.C. Chandor. Starring Oscar Isacc, Jessica Chastain, Albert Brooks. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated R. Reviewed in the Post in 2014. Now streaming on Prime.

articles.text: Frankie Muniz stars in My Dog Skip. The family-friendly film My Dog Skip, released in 2000, is a captivating story that focuses on the touching relationship between a 9-year-old boy, Willie Morris (Frankie Muniz), and his dog, a spunky Jack Russell Terrier that Willie names Skip. The film is set in Yazoo, Mississippi. The year is 1942. Willie, small for his age, is a lonely kid, often bullied by his larger classmates, especially a tough trio who take every opportunity to give him a hard time. He also has a standoffish relationship with his dad, Jack (Kevin Bacon), a gruff man, even bitter, who lost a leg in the Spanish Civil war. His mom, Ellen (Diane Lane), does her best to make Willie happy and often suggests to Jack that a dog would be the perfect companion for their isolated son. Willie of course agrees, pleads for a dog, but Jack firmly resists. Willie is about to have a birthday, and sends out an invitation to his classmates, but on the day of the scheduled party only his grandparents show up. His grandmother gives him a bowtie. But unbeknownst to Jack, his mother brings to the party a small box and inside is a sweet little terrier pup, which delights Willie, and angers Jack. But Ellen prevails. And Willie and the pooch, soon named Skip, form an immediate bond and are soon inseparable. To Willie’s delight, kids who ignored him now pay attention to Skip, especially a classmate named Rivers Applewhite (Caitlin Wachs), a cute classmate that Willie thinks is special. There are, of course, subplots. One involves thuggish moonshiners who use an abandoned burial vault in the local cemetery to hide their illegal hooch. And there’s the bullying trio who dare Willie to stay all night among the tombstones while telling him that he should be on the lookout for a witch who wanders about. There is even an awful moment when Willie, frustrated with his awkward and error-filled performance on the baseball field, gives Skip a hard swat on his nose with his baseball glove. As a result, the dog runs away. Filled with remorse, Willie begins a desperate search for Skip that ultimately involves the moonshiners. My Dog Skip, based on the memoir written by Willie Morris, a noted author and editor, unfailingly finds the sweet spot in this boy/dog narrative, demonstrating that our childhood memories, however dim, remain with us. My Dog Skip is a wonderful example. My Dog Skip. Directed by Jay Russell. Starring Frankie Muniz, Diane Lane, Kevin Bacon. 1 hr., 35 min. Rated PG. Now streaming on Netflix.
articles.title: My Dog Skip a lovely tale of a boy and his best friend

articles.text: If you see the film title of Cinderella (released in 2015) and shrug, feeling the story is all too familiar, wondering what could possibly be new in this narrative, know that you have not seen the story presented in this surprising and beautiful way. Once again it is a Disney production. This is a contemporary version of what is an iconic fairytale, fresh and engaging (with a tweak here and by the writers), but not surprising given that it’s directed by the talented English actor Kenneth Branagh. The story is simple and direct. Unlike those that have come before (the most memorable being the animated version by Disney some 65 years ago), it relies very little on special effects or computer graphics. Of course, there is the scene when Ella’s Fairy Godmother (Helena Bonham Carter) appears and turns a simple pumpkin into a startlingly beautiful, ornate coach, and the house mice slowly morph into six white steeds and two lizards become the coachmen. To its credit this film is character driven, and the wonder of Cinderella can be found in watching each individual revealed – from the very kind and enchanting Ella (Lilly James), to the cruel and sadistic Lady Tremaine (Cate Blanchett). The set up for the movie takes almost all of act one to construct. Ella is living an idyllic life with her mother (Hayley Atwell) and father (Ben Chaplin) in a gorgeous, English countryside mansion. She is embraced by her loving family and secure in her place as a much cared for daughter. Unexpectedly, sadly, Ella’s mother falls suddenly ill and dies, leaving Ella with just her father. Time passes, years slip by, and he decides to remarry, choosing a benign widow (or so he believes), Lady Tremaine, who has two daughters Ella’s age, Drisella and Anastasia (Sophia McShera and Holliday Granger). With their arrival, Ella’s life changes as act two unfolds. At first she is tolerated by her stepmother, but mocked by the sisters. But when her father dies on a business trip, Ella, now orphaned, finds her position in the household one in which she is ostracized and turned into a servant, relegated to the attic, always at the beck and call of the three women. It is they who name her Cinderella, for she sleeps by the fireplace in the den because the attic is too cold in winter. And so the story blossoms in a most compelling and captivating manner. The king (Derek Jacobi) announces that he will give a magnificent royal ball. His young son (Richard Madden), the heir and prince, insists that all of the single maidens of the kingdom must be invited. As it turns out, the prince is about to choose a bride at the ball, whether she is a commoner or titled. Naturally, Tremaine forbids Cinderella from going. That is until there is a magical moment when the fable soars. It is both glorious to watch and touching in its emotions, none of which are disguised behind computer trickery. The visuals – and they are stunning – create a magnetism that transcends and surprises, even though the outcome is solidly based on the Disney concept of living “happily ever after.” It is in getting to that moment that separates this Cinderella from all its precursors (and there have been many, to include a TV special starring Julie Andrews). As an aside, just before Ella’s mother dies, she takes her daughter’s hand and asks her to always have courage and above all else, be kind, a moral principle that Ella tries to live by, and one that is woven with sensitivity into the story. Ella is indeed courageous, and reflexively kind no matter the abuse heaped upon her by the mean-spirited Tremaine. She is also by nature innocent; but also tenacious and someone who, in every frame, is believable as she demonstrates how deeply her decency frames her life. It’s a wonderfully resonant message, brought to you once again by Disney, who has always chosen to see the world not as it is but as it should be. Cinderella. Directed by Kenneth Branagh. Starring Cate Blanchet, Lily James, Richard Madden. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG. Now streaming on Disney..

Kenneth Branagh’s Cinderella brings story to life By Chris Honoré If you see the film title of Cinderella (released in 2015) and shrug, feeling the story is all too familiar, wondering what could possibly be new in this narrative, know that you have not seen the story presented in this surprising and beautiful way. Once again it is a Disney production. This is a contemporary version of what is an iconic fairytale, fresh and engaging (with a tweak here and by the writers), but not surprising given that it’s directed by the talented English actor Kenneth Branagh. The story is simple and direct. Unlike those that have come before (the most memorable being the animated version by Disney some 65 years ago), it relies very little on special effects or computer graphics. Of course, there is the scene when Ella’s Fairy Godmother (Helena Bonham Carter) appears and turns a simple pumpkin into a startlingly beautiful, ornate coach, and the house mice slowly morph into six white steeds and two lizards become the coachmen. To its credit this film is character driven, and the wonder of Cinderella can be found in watching each individual revealed – from the very kind and enchanting Ella (Lilly James), to the cruel and sadistic Lady Tremaine (Cate Blanchett). The set up for the movie takes almost all of act one to construct. Ella is living an idyllic life with her mother (Hayley Atwell) and father (Ben Chaplin) in a gorgeous, English countryside mansion. She is embraced by her loving family and secure in her place as a much cared for daughter. Unexpectedly, sadly, Ella’s mother falls suddenly ill and dies, leaving Ella with just her father. Time passes, years slip by, and he decides to remarry, choosing a benign widow (or so he believes), Lady Tremaine, who has two daughters Ella’s age, Drisella and Anastasia (Sophia McShera and Holliday Granger). With their arrival, Ella’s life changes as act two unfolds. At first she is tolerated by her stepmother, but mocked by the sisters. But when her father dies on a business trip, Ella, now orphaned, finds her position in the household one in which she is ostracized and turned into a servant, relegated to the attic, always at the beck and call of the three women. It is they who name her Cinderella, for she sleeps by the fireplace in the den because the attic is too cold in winter. And so the story blossoms in a most compelling and captivating manner. The king (Derek Jacobi) announces that he will give a magnificent royal ball. His young son (Richard Madden), the heir and prince, insists that all of the single maidens of the kingdom must be invited. As it turns out, the prince is about to choose a bride at the ball, whether she is a commoner or titled. Naturally, Tremaine forbids Cinderella from going. That is until there is a magical moment when the fable soars. It is both glorious to watch and touching in its emotions, none of which are disguised behind computer trickery. The visuals – and they are stunning – create a magnetism that transcends and surprises, even though the outcome is solidly based on the Disney concept of living “happily ever after.” It is in getting to that moment that separates this Cinderella from all its precursors (and there have been many, to include a TV special starring Julie Andrews). As an aside, just before Ella’s mother dies, she takes her daughter’s hand and asks her to always have courage and above all else, be kind, a moral principle that Ella tries to live by, and one that is woven with sensitivity into the story. Ella is indeed courageous, and reflexively kind no matter the abuse heaped upon her by the mean-spirited Tremaine. She is also by nature innocent; but also tenacious and someone who, in every frame, is believable as she demonstrates how deeply her decency frames her life. It’s a wonderfully resonant message, brought to you once again by Disney, who has always chosen to see the world not as it is but as it should be. Cinderella. Directed by Kenneth Branagh. But with age comes wisdom, and I’ve learned there are certain things you simply avoid – like suggesting a cream rug for a household with small children and a dog, even though the client is in love with it. Sorry, Natalie. My heart is empathetic to our clients who return home from work only to discover that Fido has ripped up a mohair chair, or Fluffy has marked a silk rug. The good news is that you can have the quality and beauty you desire with smart decisions. Here are some tips to extend the life of your home if you have pets: • Make safe purchases. Opt for dark floor coverings. There are rugs made of recycled bottles that look and feel like cotton – yes, such things exist – and they clean easily. Choose wool, tightly woven fabrics, or performance leather, which is wipeable and cleanable. • Cats scratch when they feel anxious, and it’s a natural instinct. It’s how they mark their territory, and it simply feels good. The best foil is to • provide cats a place to scratch that is more appealing. Double-sided sticky tape on furniture corners can deter damage. Even though cat towers can be quite the eyesore, you can do as my client Maggie does, and stash the tower in a side room when she’s throwing a party. Her cat can lounge in its cat apartment happily, and scratch to its hearts content whenever the mood strikes. This makes Maggie – and her designer – very happy. By Pierre DuMont In 2015 I made a trip to the Northern Rhone to explore some of the incredible Syrahs and Viogniers that are made in that region. One of the highlights of the trip was the discovery of the wines of Pierre Gaillard. In 1987 he established his winery in the medieval town of Malleval in the appellation of Condrieu. Since then he has expanded by creating estates in the south of France in Banyuls-sur-Mer and in Faugeres. The Northern Rhone appellations of Cote Rotie and Condrieu are some of the most challenging places to make wine in the world. The vines are situated on steep slopes plunging down toward the Rhone. It is only the extensive terracing that keeps the entire hillside from sliding into the river. The soil is made of decomposing schist and granite. In a throwback to earlier days, sometimes Gaillard resorts to plowing the soils between the vines with a horse-drawn plow. This is definitely an old-school traditional estate. The only modern touch seems to be the beautiful watercolor labels on the bottles. If the only Syrahs and Viogniers you have had are from California, you are in for a change of pace. The climate of the Northern Rhone is much colder than California. That results in the wines having more acid and structure. When Viognier The vines of Condrieu roll down to the Rhone river. is grown in a warm climate it often becomes dull and flabby, and Syrah becomes too fruity and sweet. The Rhone versions have incredible balance between fruit and acid, and also have an earthiness and minerality you don’t find elsewhere. The Pierre Gaillard wines are part of the Jack Edwards Collection and are certainly worth searching out. (jackedwardscollection.com) • 2019 Pierre Gaillard Condrieu, $45 I could just swirl and sniff this wine for an hour. It is full and textured with an elegant nose of citrus, honeysuckle, wet stones and peaches. This Condrieu is rich, medium to full-bodied and impeccably balanced with lots of pear and apricot fruit on the palate. This is drinking beautifully, so no need to cellar. • 2020 Pierre Gaillard In Dolio Chardonnay, $20 This wine came as a surprise to me. Chardonnay grapes are not allowed in Condrieu, but are allowed in the adjacent area of Collines Rhodaniennes. This amphore fermented wine has a well-defined citrus-driven bouquet that is nicely controlled and opens in the glass with time. The palate is crisp on the entry with lemon and a touch of orange zest, with a finish that is controlled and refined. While this is an enjoyable wine, my advice to the Rhone winemakers would be to stick with your wonderful native grapes. The world just doesn’t need another Chardonnay. • 2019 Pierre Gaillard Crozes Hermitage, $24 Crozes hermitage is the baby sister of the famed Hermitage hill near Tain. Like Hermitage, it is made from 100% Syrah but has a softer profile. This bottle shows charming floral notes alongside hints of black olives and ripe cherries. It is medium bodied, creamy and fairly concentrated yet silky and fine, with hints of mocha building on the finish. Would be great with a beef stew or braised veal shanks. • 2017 Pierre Gaillard Saint Joseph Clos de Cuminalle, $30 Perfumed, elegant and alluring, Gaillard’s 2017 St. Joseph smells of fresh-cut flowers, blackberry pie and hints of licorice. It builds on the palate and has good richness, but it shines for its elegance and subtlety. Drink over the next decade, preferably serving with a nice roasted leg of lamb. articles.text: Weather forecasts had the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group a little uncertain on Wednesday, March 2, but extra layers of clothes were soon unnecessary. It was a lovely day for a walk. A strong turnout of 36 walkers and one K-9 best friend showed up at the Exedra for some morning exercise. The Post had reported two weeks before that there was a retaining wall project under construction on San Carlos Avenue, so the walkers headed off down Magnolia Avenue, past the new Piedmont High theater. The sidewalk in front of the building was completely cleared and all the fences and construction equipment were gone and the beauty of this new piece of Piedmont High was fully on display. The walkers took a side trip on the 400 block of El Cerrito Avenue which goes directly to Witter Field. The street forms a U as it merges into Jerome, and soon they were back at Magnolia and a short walk later to the lower portion of the divided San CarIos Avenue. At the far end of the block, near Oakland Avenue, they came to the completed, new portion of the wall. It is a hundred feet or so long, and blends in nicely with the rest of the walk. It was agreed that the construction company did a nice job, and they stopped for a group photo with Stella Houston holding the Post. The sheer number of walkers obscured the wall itself (see photo). The walkers carefully crossed Oakland Avenue and continued on San Carlos, observing tree work and house remodeling along the way. San Carlos ends at Blair Avenue, which quickly becomes Ricardo Avenue. Next was Cambridge Way and the group took it to Manor Drive where they went up and down the parallel streets of Manor and York Drive, and Ricardo and Monticello Avenues, with Cambridge Way and Arroyo Avenue providing a bridge between them. On Cambridge the walkers were charmed by a home built in 1925 in a storybook design. It has a “witch’s cap” turret above the front door that the walkers felt Hansel and Gretel would have liked too. The walkers went up Monticello to the Lorita Avenue culde-sac looking for the bottom of a very hidden pathway, but they walked past it without seeing it. The group continued up Monticello and then onto Park Way when the road takes a hard left and Monticello becomes Park Way. They admired the beautiful cedar shake shingle homes across from Dracena Park. Many were built in 1908 by people moving to the area after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake. There was also a huge evergreen tree in the yard of a home near Dracena Avenue that the walkers admired. Near the top of Park was opportunity to visit one more seldom walked street, Waldo Avenue, one-block long with lovely homes and blossoming trees on what was once the back side of the home of Walter Blair, the first European settler of what is now Piedmont. At Blair Avenue they went a half block to Highland and a short walk back to the center of town. In all it had been about a three mile walk with many new and old friends on a delightful, late winter morning. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Dr. Paul Farmer The world has suffered a great loss in the passing of Dr. Paul Farmer, Co-founder and Chief Strategist of Partners in Health (PIH) and Chair of the Department of Global Health and Social Medicine at Harvard Medical School — and a friend to so many of us. There are not enough accolades to describe the life of a man who dedicated himself so completely to solving the world’s greatest problems of poverty, inequality, and global health disparities. Despite a book about his life and work (Tracy Kidder’s Mountains Beyond Mountains), a film (Bending the Arc), his own published works (Pathologies of Power, Partner to the Poor, To Repair the World, Reimagining Global Health, and more), and countless writings, speeches, and awards, it is impossible to fully convey the loss that is being felt around the world. I first met Dr. Farmer when I was a medical student rotating at Brigham & Women’s Hospital in Boston. He was a resident then, and it was during an on-call dinner in the cafeteria when I learned of his work in Haiti. Months later, he received the prestigious MacArthur “Genius Grant,” and yet he would always remain down-to-earth and approachable to medical students. During my residency at the Brigham, Dr. Farmer was the infectious disease fellow who helped us on tough clinical cases at all hours of the day and night. Even then, he was the one who called attention to the unaddressed issues impacting a patient’s medical care. During one memorable conversation about house staff occupational exposures, he pointed out to me the greater challenges faced by less visible healthcare workers, whose choice of profession may not have been as intentional as our own. Photo Courtesy of Harvard University Dr. Farmer’s insights and the life he led by example were an unconscious influence during my formative years of training and may have helped guide my own career decisions that did not follow traditional metrics for success. I was grateful that both my work and the Brigham alumni community afforded me opportunities to stay in touch with him periodically throughout the years. Last year the American Medical Women’s Association was deeply honored to have Dr. Farmer deliver one of our Annual Gala Keynotes. It had been just over a year into the pandemic and eight months after the death of George Floyd, a time which he aptly characterized as one of “awakening and loss… a tectonic level of change.” He reminded us of the importance of resisting a “guild mentality, in order to fight for what our patients deserve and what we need to serve them.” Most importantly, he posed this question, “Where do we go as a healing profession in the midst of all this pain?” His heartfelt answer would become a guiding message for us: “…leadership, allyship, and looking out for each other are a big part of what we most need right now. We are certainly humans before heroes, but many of those gathering virtually for the AMWA meeting are nonetheless heroes to me, working as you do to make medicine truly humane and inclusive but also clearly on the right side of history’s ledger.” At only 62 years of age, Dr. Farmer’s work was far from over. And so, it is left to those of us who remain to follow the path that he forged, to carry on his work to fight inequality on behalf of not only our patients but those less visible in all corners of the world. Dr. Eliza Lo Chin is Executive Director of American Medical Women’s Association and a Piedmont resident.

articles.text: William Joseph Sullivan, 94, passed away peacefully surrounded by his loving family on Saturday, January 29, 2022. He lived a life of service to others and will be greatly missed. Bill was born in Anaconda, Montana on June 16, 1927, the son of Joseph Michael and Alice Marie Peacher Sullivan. In 1945, he graduated from Anaconda High School and enlisted in the United States Army. Bill proudly served as a T-5 Topical Draftsman in Korea with the First Infantry Regiment of the 6th Army Division. Following the Korean War, he returned to his home state and earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Pharmacy and a Master’s of Science degree in Chemistry from the University of Montana. In 1954, Bill married Anaconda native Helen Marie Ryan. They moved to Ann Arbor, Michigan, where Bill continued his studies at the University of Michigan and earned a Ph.D. in Medicinal Chemistry. As a young scientist, he began his career serving as a research chemist for Shell Development Company and moved his family to California where they lived for 60 years. Dr. Sullivan entered into business as a pharmacist and owned and operated various pharmacies, including the Montclair Pharmacy Dr. William Sullivan, the longtime owner of Montclair Pharmacy, passed away on January 29 at age 94. in Oakland. His wife, Helen, joined him in their business pursuits, and all members of their family worked at the stores over a period of 50 years. The Sullivans were generous supporters of many charities and loyal parishioners at Corpus Christi Church. Always active, he enjoyed many painting and construction projects. Together with his son, he built a family vacation home at Lake-of-the-Pines in Auburn, CA. He was a longtime member of the University of Montana’s Grizzly Riders where he earned the “butt buster” award for the most hours in a saddle during their annual horseback rides. Dr. Sullivan retired from the Montclair Pharmacy at age 85 and happily returned to his roots in Montana alongside his devoted wife. He enjoyed the last nine years working on his ranch, following business and political news, managing real estate, and spending time with family and friends. He valued education and endowed scholarships at the University of Montana and the University of Michigan. Most of all, he had an incredible work ethic, was a loyal caretaker, generous patriarch, and devoted Catholic. He is survived by his two daughters, Laurice Salamack (Joe) of Johnstown, NY, and Mary Alice McNeil (Tim) of Piedmont; daughter-in-law Carol Sullivan of Grass Valley, CA; five grandchildren, Ryan Sullivan, Kelly Salamack Casey (Kevin) and Allison Salamack Dodd-o (Joseph), William and Thomas McNeil, and numerous nieces and nephews. He is predeceased by his wife Helen Marie in 2014; son, Joseph Michael Sullivan II in 2020; and sister Shirley Sullivan Kudzia in 2017. A memorial mass will be held at Corpus Christi Church, 322 St. James Drive, Piedmont, on March 19, 2022 at 11:00 AM. In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to Corpus Christi Church.

articles.text: At the base of the hillside framing Blair Park is a majestic California bay laurel. This huge tree is part of the Umbellularia californica family. It is a native, evergreen tree found along the western coastline of California and southern Oregon, usually in bottomland sites, along streams, or dry rocky areas. It is a sturdy tree known for its ability to withstand strong coastal winds. Its leaves are oblong shaped with a smooth, leathery texture. When the leaves are crushed, they have a strong, pungent odor. Native American Indian tribes used the leaves for medicinal remedies and to season their food. Today, these leaves are still dried and used in cooking. In the late winter and early spring, the tree blooms with small, yellowish-green flowers. The wood from the tree is highly valued for its beauty and can be made to make wood furCalifornia Bay Laurel. niture and moldings. Additionally, wood carvers often use the burls from California bay laurels to make decorative objects. These burls are rounded outgrowths on the tree trunks and branches Photo by Brian Mahany which are considered beautiful. This California bay laurel was designated as a Heritage Tree in 2021 and was nominated by Marge Blackwell and the Van Slyke family. Go out and explore your Piedmont neighborhood to look for a remarkable tree to nominate as a Heritage Tree. Nominations are due by March 18, 2022 and will be evaluated on their aesthetic, educational, or historical merits by a Park Commission subcommittee. At the April 6 Park Commission meeting, commissioners will vote to approve the selected nominations. This year’s selections will be announced at the City Arbor Day festivities on April 28. Forms are available on the City’s website on its Heritage Tree page at https://www.piedmont.ca.gov/cms/One.aspx?- portalId=13659823&pag eId=17970894. For more information, please contact Piedmont Parks Manager Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov or 510- 420-3064.
